findings.source_passage: The isolated subterraneousness of the cabin made a certain humming silence to reign there, though it was hooped round by all the roar of the elements.
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'Ere knocking at his state-room'
findings.why_it_matters: This sentence is one of Melville's most rhetorically distinctive in the chapter — the paradox of silence inside roar is an interpretive keystone for Ahab's isolation and the chapter's atmosphere. Its loss erases a signature voice moment.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the sentence verbatim between the lamp/shadow description and the musket revelation.

findings.source_passage: Starbuck was an honest, upright man; but out of Starbuck's heart, at that instant when he saw the muskets, there strangely evolved an evil thought; but so blent with its neutral or good accompaniments that for the instant he hardly knew it for itself.
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'Ere knocking at his state-room', final sentences
findings.why_it_matters: This sentence is critically central: it stages the ambiguous moral emergence of the murder impulse ('so blent with its neutral or good accompaniments'). The critical tradition repeatedly cites it as defining Melville's psychological realism here. Its complete absence is a major interpretive loss.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore this sentence verbatim after the musket rack description; it is too interpretively weighty to compress away.

findings.source_passage: and in this very Typhoon, did he not swear that he would have no lightning-rods?
findings.why_it_matters: The lightning-rod refusal is a key motif linking back to the corpusants scene; its omission from Starbuck's case against Ahab thins the thematic accumulation of Ahab's recklessness.
findings.suggested_fix: Re-insert the lightning-rod question in Starbuck's interior litany of Ahab's madnesses.

findings.source_passage: What, then, remains? The land is hundreds of leagues away, and locked Japan the nearest.
findings.source_locator: Starbuck's interior monologue, near end before the musket is raised
findings.why_it_matters: The rhetorical question 'What, then, remains?' and the geographical isolation ('locked Japan the nearest') give the monologue its climactic shape and underline Starbuck's utter lawlessness of situation; the draft skips from the fool passage directly to 'I stand alone' losing this pivot.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'What, then, remains? The land is hundreds of leagues away, and locked Japan the nearest' as a transitional line before 'I stand alone here upon an open sea.'

findings.source_passage: Great God, where art Thou? Shall I? shall I?
findings.source_locator: Starbuck's final words before Ahab's voice breaks through, inside the cabin-door monologue
findings.why_it_matters: This direct address to God is the emotional and theological apex of the chapter; its absence means the draft's Starbuck shifts immediately from 'Oh Mary! Mary!' to Ahab's dream-voice without the crucial moment of divine appeal and paralysis.
findings.suggested_fix: Insert 'Great God, where art Thou? Shall I? shall I?—' between the family cry and the wind-report line.

findings.source_passage: if this ship come to any deadly harm; and come to deadly harm, my soul swears this ship will, if Ahab have his way.
findings.source_locator: Starbuck's interior monologue, 'wilful murderer of thirty men' passage
findings.why_it_matters: The phrase 'my soul swears this ship will' is Starbuck's prophetic self-conviction — interpretively it clinches his foreknowledge of doom and the moral logic of the monologue; its loss flattens the passage into generic worry.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the 'wilful murderer of thirty men' sentence with the 'my soul swears' clause intact.

summary: The draft drops two high-severity signature passages — the 'isolated subterraneousness' sentence and the 'evil thought so blent' sentence — along with four medium-severity losses (lightning-rods, 'What then remains / locked Japan', 'Great God where art Thou / Shall I shall I', and 'my soul swears this ship will'), collectively gutting the chapter's psychological, theological, and atmospheric core.
